knowledgeNodes.name: Theoretical Probability
knowledgeNodes.definition: The probability of an event calculated based on the ratio of favorable outcomes to total possible outcomes in a sample space, assuming all outcomes are equally likely. Formula: P(E) = number of favorable outcomes / total number of outcomes.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: determine the theoretical probability, Pi (i.e., a value from 0 to 1), of each outcome of a discrete sample space, recognize that the sum of the probabilities of the outcomes is 1, and solve related problems.

knowledgeNodes.name: Experimental Probability and Law of Large Numbers
knowledgeNodes.nameEn: Experimental Probability and Law of Large Numbers
knowledgeNodes.definition: Experimental probability is the ratio of the number of times an event occurs to the total number of trials. As the number of trials increases, the experimental probability tends to approach the theoretical probability (Law of Large Numbers).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: determine, through investigation using class-generated data and technology-based simulation models, the tendency of experimental probability to approach theoretical probability as the number of trials in an experiment increases.

options.label: A
options.text: Experimental probability always equals theoretical probability after 10 trials.
options.feedbackWrong: Not always; it varies but tends to stabilize with many trials.

options.label: B
options.text: Experimental probability becomes more reliable as the number of trials increases.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! As trials increase, experimental probability approaches theoretical probability.

options.feedbackWrong: It can be greater or less, but tends to approach the theoretical value.

questions.stem: In a deck of cards, what is the probability of NOT drawing an ace? Explain your reasoning using the complement rule.
questions.successCriteria: Student calculates 1 - (4/52) = 48/52 = 12/13 and explains complement concept.
questions.ossdExpectation: determine the theoretical probability, P (i.e., a value from 0 to 1), of each outcome of a discrete sample space (e.g., in games of chance, in applying for scholarships, for the results of an experiment), recognize that the sum of the probabilities of the outcomes is 1, and solve related problems.
questions.alignmentNote: Complementary probability is part of solving related problems under SE A1.3.
questions.stemIntent: Check ability to apply complement rule and justify.
questions.commonMisconception: Student may add probabilities incorrectly or not understand complement.
questions.rubric: Full marks: correct probability (12/13) and clear explanation using complement: P(not ace) = 1 - P(ace) = 1 - 4/52 = 48/52 = 12/13. Partial: correct probability but weak explanation.
questions.sampleStrongAnswer: The probability of not drawing an ace is 1 minus the probability of drawing an ace. Since P(ace) = 4/52 = 1/13, then P(not ace) = 1 - 1/13 = 12/13. This uses the complement rule.

reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student may think the probability is just the number of favorable outcomes without considering the total, or may invert the fraction favorable/total.

miniLesson.explain: Theoretical probability is calculated using the formula: P(event) = number of favorable outcomes / total number of possible outcomes. All outcomes must be equally likely. For example, in a fair die, each face has probability 1/6.
miniLesson.example: For a fair six-sided die, the probability of rolling a 3 is 1/6 because there is 1 favorable outcome (rolling a 3) and 6 total possible outcomes.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of a fraction: favorable over total. Favorable on top, total on bottom.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the probability of rolling an even number on a fair six-sided die?
A bag has 20 marbles: 4 blue, 6 orange, 7 green, 3 purple. What is the probability of drawing a green marble?
What is the probability of NOT drawing an ace from a standard deck of 52 cards?

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly answered question about experimental probability approaching theoretical probability.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students often think experimental probability is always equal to theoretical probability or does not change as trials increase.

miniLesson.explain: Experimental probability is the ratio of the number of times an event occurs to the total number of trials. According to the Law of Large Numbers, as the number of trials increases, the experimental probability tends to get closer to the theoretical probability. For example, when rolling a fair die many times, the experimental probability of rolling a 3 will approach 1/6.
miniLesson.example: If you roll a die 10 times, you might get a 3 twice (experimental probability = 2/10 = 0.2). After 1000 rolls, the experimental probability will likely be very close to 1/6 ≈ 0.167.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of a dartboard: with few throws, your hits are scattered, but with many throws, your hit percentage stabilizes near your skill level.

guidedPractice.prompt: After flipping a fair coin 100 times, you got heads 50 times. What is the experimental probability of heads?
You draw a card from a standard deck 13 times with replacement and get a face card 3 times. What is the experimental probability of drawing a face card?
Explain how the Law of Large Numbers applies to rolling a fair die. Use the terms experimental probability and theoretical probability.
guidedPractice.answer: The theoretical probability of rolling a 3 is 1/6. After many rolls, the experimental probability (number of 3s / total rolls) will get closer and closer to 1/6.

From a standard deck of 52 playing cards, what is the theoretical probability of drawing a face card? Show your calculation and simplify if possible.
questions.rubric: Accept 12/52 = 3/13. Student must state there are 12 face cards (J, Q, K) out of 52 total cards, and reduce fraction.

retestCards.passRule: Answer Q1 correctly and Q2 with correct answer and justification.

questions.rubric: Student correctly states that according to the Law of Large Numbers, as the number of trials increases, the experimental probability approaches the theoretical probability.
